Memory and speed tips in R

Good memories, good times

Using large dataset often comes with memory or runtime issues. Here we’ll run through some ways that can reduce these issues. It’s based in R, but many of the principles will apply when using Python or other software.

Even if you’re not having memory issues, good memory management is a good habit to get into!

First, let’s create some data. This will be used to demonstrate some of the benefits of writing performant code.

library("tidyverse")  
── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
rcat <- function(n, levels, p, factor = TRUE) {
  x <- sample(x = levels, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = p)
  if (factor) x <- factor(x, levels = levels)
  x
}  

set.seed(42)  

N <- 10000

dataset <- tibble(
  patient_id = seq_len(N),
  age = as.integer(rnorm(N, 65, 15)),
  sex = rcat(N, c("female", "male"), p = c(0.5,0.5)),
  diabetes = as.logical(rbinom(N, 1, 0.2)), # (swap as.logical for as.integer to get a 0/1 flag instead)
  hba1c = round(rnorm(N, 25 + 10*diabetes, 10), 1),
  hba1c_over60 = if_else(hba1c > 60, "yes", "no"),
  death_date = as.Date("2021-01-01") +
    as.integer({.x <- runif(N, 0, 3000 - 1000*diabetes); if_else(.x < 366, .x, NA)}) 
)

print(dataset)
# A tibble: 10,000 × 7
   patient_id   age sex    diabetes hba1c hba1c_over60 death_date
        <int> <int> <fct>  <lgl>    <dbl> <chr>        <date>    
 1          1    85 female FALSE     19.1 no           NA        
 2          2    56 male   FALSE     22.8 no           NA        
 3          3    70 male   FALSE     25.8 no           NA        
 4          4    74 female FALSE     30.4 no           NA        
 5          5    71 male   FALSE     32.6 no           NA        
 6          6    63 male   FALSE     24.2 no           NA        
 7          7    87 male   FALSE     29.5 no           NA        
 8          8    63 male   FALSE     43.8 no           NA        
 9          9    95 female TRUE      40.1 no           2021-05-20
10         10    64 male   FALSE     21.2 no           NA        
# ℹ 9,990 more rows

Measure for measure

Before you optimise anything, find out what’s actually slow. Intuition about R performance is notoriously unreliable — the bottleneck is very often not where you’d guess. The golden rule: optimise the slow bit, not the bit you assume is slow. A day spent hand-optimising a function that accounts for 2% of runtime is a day wasted.

There are three questions worth answering, each with its own tool.

Where is the time going? {profvis} runs your code and produces an interactive flame graph, paired with a line-by-line source view, showing exactly which lines cost the most time and memory. Wrap any block of code in profvis({...}) and explore the result. (Your code has to run long enough to be sampled — profvis takes a snapshot every few milliseconds, so anything that finishes in under a millisecond gives it nothing to measure.) Below we profile a small three-step pipeline — simulate a cohort, compute regional means, fit a model. Which step would you guess is slowest? The flame graph makes it obvious: nearly all the time is in fit_model() — specifically lm() building its model matrix and calling lm.fit() — and almost none in simulating the data or the group-wise summary. That’s the whole point: measure, don’t assume.

library("profvis")

# profvis only shows its line-by-line source view when the profiled code lives
# in a file (source references are otherwise stripped when a doc is rendered),
# so we write the pipeline out to a file first, then profile it
writeLines(c(
  "simulate_cohort <- function(n) data.frame(",
  "  patient_id = seq_len(n),",
  "  age        = rnorm(n, 65, 15),",
  "  region     = sample(LETTERS[1:8], n, replace = TRUE),",
  "  hba1c      = rnorm(n, 30, 10)",
  ")",
  "",
  "regional_means <- function(d) tapply(d$hba1c, d$region, mean)",
  "",
  "fit_model <- function(d) lm(hba1c ~ age + region, data = d)",
  "",
  "cohort <- simulate_cohort(4e6)",
  "means  <- regional_means(cohort)",
  "fit    <- fit_model(cohort)"
), "profvis_demo.R")

profvis(source("profvis_demo.R", local = TRUE, keep.source = TRUE))

Which of two approaches is faster? {bench} times competing implementations and, crucially, checks that they all return identical results — so you can’t accidentally declare a “faster” version that’s actually computing the wrong thing. (This is the key advantage over the older {microbenchmark}.)

library("bench")

bench::mark(
  base    = tapply(dataset$hba1c, dataset$sex, mean, na.rm = TRUE),
  dplyr   = dataset |> group_by(sex) |> summarise(m = mean(hba1c, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(m),
  check   = FALSE  # set TRUE when outputs are directly comparable
)
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 base          136µs    169µs     5901.     397KB     4.79
2 dplyr         786µs    849µs     1176.     2.5MB    21.0

Where is the memory going? Rprof(memory.profiling = TRUE) (base R, always available) records memory allocation alongside timing, and {profmem} reports total allocations for a block of code — useful for catching hidden copies (see Copy-on-modify below).

Note

{profvis} and {bench} are included in the R image v3 but not v2. If you’re on v2 (or any image without them), the base-R fallbacks are system.time() for crude timing and Rprof() / summaryRprof() for sampling profiles — less pretty, but always there.

Stay classy

A vector in R belongs to a class. The class determines what set of values are valid for the vector. Classes can be simple, like a integer or character, or more complicated like datetime or (there is a lot more to classes in R, as they apply to any object, not just vectors. But i’m not covering that here).

Let’s look at the class for each vector (column) in our dataset:

map_chr(dataset, class)
  patient_id          age          sex     diabetes        hba1c hba1c_over60 
   "integer"    "integer"     "factor"    "logical"    "numeric"  "character" 
  death_date 
      "Date"

Each class is actually just one of four different atomic types: logical, integer, double, and character. All classes belong to a particular type under-the-hood, with some additional rules determining how each value should be represented and processed.

For example, a factor class is just an integer type in disguise, because each specific string in the factor has been mapped from an integer. For example, the sex column in the dataset is just an integer-type vector but with a rule saying “if the type value is 1 then the class value is the string ‘female’; if the type value is 2 then the class value is the string ‘male’”. Similarly, Dates are doubles in disguise, with a rule saying “if the type value is x then the class value is x days since 01-01-1970”.

Let’s look at the type for each column in our dataset:

map_chr(dataset, typeof)
  patient_id          age          sex     diabetes        hba1c hba1c_over60 
   "integer"    "integer"    "integer"    "logical"     "double"  "character" 
  death_date 
    "double"

Each type uses a different amount of memory to store its values. Generally speaking, the memory footprint from low to high is: logical = integer < double = character. Before we look at the memory use for each column, a quick aside on measuring it: the base object.size() is convenient but can mislead — it ignores memory shared between objects, and it reports some compact objects as if they were fully materialised. {lobstr}’s obj_size() (in the v2 and v3 images) is more accurate, so we use that here. Let’s look at the memory use (in bytes) for each column in our 10^{4} row dataset:

map_dbl(dataset, \(x) as.numeric(lobstr::obj_size(x)))
  patient_id          age          sex     diabetes        hba1c hba1c_over60 
         680        40048        40560        40048        80048        80160 
  death_date 
       80272

Notice that patient_id comes out far smaller than the other columns, even though it has just as many values. That’s because seq_len(N) is stored as a compact “ALTREP” integer sequence — R keeps only the start, end and step, not all 10^{4} values. object.size() would have reported it at the full materialised size (around 40 KB); obj_size() sees the truth (a few hundred bytes). A good reminder that what you measure depends on how you measure.

If you’re storing values as one type when they could be stored as a lower-memory type, then it’s usually worth re-typing.

The most likely savings in R you’ll find in a routine analysis in R are swapping from a numeric (double) to an integer class, and from character to factor. Each of these will roughly halve the memory allocation for each vector.

We can see this in action if we convert hba1c_over60 vector from character to a factor or a logical vector:

# character
lobstr::obj_size(dataset$hba1c_over60)
80.16 kB
# factor (integer, with some overheads for mapping integer to character values)
lobstr::obj_size(as.factor(dataset$hba1c_over60))
40.56 kB
# logical
lobstr::obj_size(dataset$hba1c_over60 == "yes")
40.05 kB

Some tips:

  • If a column contains only integer values, type it as an integer not a double. It’s common for integers to sneakily convert back to doubles. For example, if x is an integer, then y <- x + 1 is a double, because 1 is a double and combining an integer and a double will give a double. Instead, use y <- x + 1L which is an integer because 1L is an integer.

  • A vector can have only one data type. Appending a vector with greater precision to a vector of lower precision – for instance 2.0 (double) instead of an 2L (integer) – will lead to the entire column converting from integer to double. This fact is obvious to most R users but its easy for it to happen without realising, when using bind_rows() or c() calls for instance.

  • R’s standard integer type maxes out at .Machine$integer.max – about 2.1 billion (231 − 1). Go above that and it silently overflows to NA (with a warning). Patient counts won’t get near it, but certain ID schemes, or a product of two large numbers, can. The {bit64} package (in the v2 and v3 images) provides an integer64 type for whole numbers up to about 9.2 × 1018, in the same 8 bytes a double would use.

  • If a column contains only a few different string values, it’s usually better to convert it from a character to a factor. In fact, because there is no free-text info in OpenSAFELY, in theory all string-type variables, including derived variables, should only contain values from a known set, and so could all be represented as factors. But in practice this might not be simple to enforce, and might be actively unhelpful if lots of theoretically possible values are not actually represented. So some character variables are permissible. Use your judgement. One caveat worth spelling out: converting to a factor only saves memory when the column has few distinct values relative to its length. Converting a high-cardinality column — one where almost every value is unique, like an ID — to a factor stores a full integer code for every row plus a complete table of levels, so it can cost more memory (and speed), not less.

  • Beware default behaviours when reading in text-based files (eg csv, tsv, txt, etc) as data.frames.

  • For heavy purely numeric work — lots of repeated row/column indexing, or feeding data into matrix algebra — consider holding it in a plain matrix rather than a data.frame/tibble. A data frame carries per-column overhead and its [ indexing is comparatively slow; a matrix is one contiguous block. (This only applies when every column shares a single type, of course.)

Trim the fat

R global environments, and the objects within, will often be carrying more baggage than is needed. If you’re running into memory issues, get rid of any large objects in memory that you don’t need. Or better, avoid creating them in the first place.

Objects can be removed from environments using rm(). This allows the memory it occupies to be used later on if needed. It doesn’t actually give the memory back to the operating system, but that’s ok because the memory is still available within R. You could also run gc() (garbage collection) to completely free-up the memory, but this is usually unnecessary (Note: ask the tech team whether this might have any benefits to the wider running of OS!)

Another option is to write code that loads or processes data in functions, or within a local({...}) call. In this case, none of the intermediate objects can saved to the global environment, avoid clutter and the need to explicitly remove using rm().

Even if you need an object, you might not need all the things inside it. Data frames containing superfluous columns is an obvious example. If you no longer need a column in your dataset, get rid of it if it’s part of a memory-intensive script.

Another culprit is model objects, like the objects created when executing a glm() or coxph() call. You can often make these objects smaller by using options like data=FALSE, x=FALSE, and model=FALSE in the model call, but this might not be the primary issue if the object is capturing a large environment; see the introduction to {butcher} for more details about how model objects can become bloated and how you can deal with it.

Some tips:

  • Only import columns that get used. Remove unused columns or rows.
  • Avoid creating columns that contain the same information as other columns, just in a different format. Defer prettification until needed.

  • Store vectors that only containing a single value as global variables, or in a list, rather than as a column in a dataset that repeats the same value.

  • Remove large objects from memory if they’re no longer needed using rm().

  • Avoid storing the same information inside multiple datasets. Use look-up tables instead, and join the data on when needed. This might result in slightly slower code, but could massively lower the memory footprint.

  • Use function calls or `local()` calls to avoid intermediate objects being saved into the global environment.

  • Rather than importing data at the top of a script, import only when the data are needed.

Vectorisation

Many operations in R are vectorised. c(1,2,3) + c(3,2,1) is an example of a vectorised operation; we don’t need to explicitly loop through the 3 elements of the vectors, add them together elementally, and then concatenate the results to arrive at c(4,4,4). Instead, the + operator handles all that for us, in a fast and efficient way (usually using a lower-level language like C++). For simple operations on simple objects, vectorisation usually happens automatically, perhaps without users even realising. But sometimes you have to work a little to make it happen. This might requires a bit of effort, but is well worth the reward.

Doing this properly usually means finding a way to use in-built vectorized functions to do what you need to do. If you end up using Vectorize() to make a non-vectorised function a vectorised function, then this probably won’t be as fast (it just allows the function to accept vectors instead of atomic objects and return element-wise operations on them, but it’s not taking advantage of the speed of properly vectorised operations).

Basically, if a function can take a vector or matrix (as opposed to a list!) as an input, then it is probably vectorised. Use these for column-wise operations in you dataset!

Copy that

Under the hood, R uses copy-on-modify: when you change an object, R will often make a fresh copy of it rather than editing it in place. Most of the time you never notice. But it has one notorious consequence — growing an object inside a loop is quadratically slow and quadratically memory-hungry.

Every time you run x <- c(x, i) (or df <- bind_rows(df, new_row), or result <- rbind(result, ...)) inside a loop, R allocates a brand-new, slightly-bigger object and copies the entire contents across. Do that n times and you’ve copied roughly n²/2 elements in total — and the benchmark below shows just how brutal that is.

There are three fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Vectorise it if you can (see above) — then there’s no loop at all.

  2. Pre-allocate the result to its final size and fill it in: x <- numeric(n), then x[i] <- ... inside the loop. No copying, because the object never changes size.

  3. If you don’t know the final size, or you’re building up rows, collect into a list and combine once at the end — purrr::list_rbind(), dplyr::bind_rows(), or data.table::rbindlist() on the whole list. That’s one allocation instead of n.

The cost is not subtle. Here are all three approaches building the vector of squares from the profiling example:

library("bench")

grow       <- function(n) { x <- c(); for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- c(x, i^2); x }
prealloc   <- function(n) { x <- numeric(n); for (i in seq_len(n)) x[i] <- i^2; x }
vectorised <- function(n) seq_len(n)^2

bench::mark(
  grow       = grow(20000),
  prealloc   = prealloc(20000),
  vectorised = vectorised(20000)
)
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 grow          262ms    263ms      3.80    1.49GB     7.61
2 prealloc      511µs  551.3µs   1804.    174.19KB     2.00
3 vectorised     16µs   17.9µs  50711.    234.47KB    15.2

The growing version allocates well over a gigabyte to produce a vector that occupies a couple of hundred kilobytes — almost all of it copies that are made and immediately thrown away. (Note that bench::mark() checks all three return identical results by default, so we know we’re comparing like with like.)

If you suspect an object is being copied when you didn’t expect it, tracemem() will print a message every time R duplicates it:

x <- 1:10
tracemem(x)
x[1] <- 99L      # prints a "tracemem[...] ->" message: a copy happened here
untracemem(x)

This is also the deep reason {data.table} is so memory-light: its := operator modifies a table in place, without copying. Where a dplyr mutate() conceptually produces a whole new data frame, dt[, newcol := ...] edits the existing one. On a multi-gigabyte table, that difference can be the difference between an action that runs and one that falls over. More on data.table below.

Loops

If you can’t vectorise some loop-like operation, that doesn’t mean there aren’t efficiencies to be had.

If you use a for-loop when you could instead use the lapply()-family or purrr::map()-family functions, then you should use the latter. These aren’t vectorised, in the sense that they’re not doing vector operations in some lower-level language. They’re still repeatedly calling a function on each element in the list. However, they still provide some advantages as they automatically handle memory allocation efficiently (as they know the size of the list to be returned) and don’t leave behind temporary variables in your environment. You can do this with for-loops too, but you have to think about it more.

More threading, less dreading

AKA: more splitting, less quitting. AKA: parallelisation!

Parallelisation allows multiple processes to be run at once on different processors (or “cores”, or “threads”), which usually means things run faster.

Parallelisation in OpenSAFELY can be split into two distinct categories: within-action and across-action parallelisation.

Within-action parallelisation will be a familiar approach to many analysts – use {foreach}/{doparallel}, {future.apply}, {furrr}, or similar to access multiple cores and run things in parallel, within a single script. While you can spread you processes across different cores in a single action, there is still a hard memory limit for each action which is the same regardless of the number of cores you’re using.

Between-action parallelisation is a complementary option in OpenSAFELY. Any two actions in an OS study pipeline that are not on the same (directed) path can be run in parallel. OS will automatically run actions in parallel if there is enough compute capacity. Users can exploit this to benefit from parallelisation without having to worry about setting up parallelisation within a script. Using action parameters will be helpful in this scenario (there’s no OS documentation on parameters for R actions!). One benefit of this approach is that if you can add a new parallelisable slice without having to re-run all slices. For example, say you want to run a model against threes outcomes. You set up your pipeline to run each model in a separate action, each with the same dependencies, using an action parameter to set the value of the outcome. You run these actions, then decide you want to add a fourth outcome. IN this case, you can just add a additional action to run against that outcome, and leave the other actions untouched. If instead you had set the three models to run within a single action (within-action parallelisation), then you’d have to re-run all models in order to run the fourth model.

You can find the number of threads available by running parallel::detectCores(). This will probably be different on your local machine than on an OS backend, so you may want to use a different number of cores depending on whether you’re running running on your machine (or codespaces) versus running against the real data. And be considerate! When running on the server, don’t access so many cores for a single action that other users will suffer. If you need more than 8 cores to get close to a reasonable run time, then you should make other changes.

Operations that are amenable to parallelisation include: exact matching; bootstrapping; multiple imputation; running the same type of analysis across different inputs (exposures, outcomes, adjustment sets, subgroups, etc); most flavours of sensitivity analyses, …

Remember that parallelisation scales well – if parallelisation doesn’t seem to make much difference (or is slightly worse) in 10k rows, it might still bring big benefits in 10m rows.

{data.table} / {dtplyr}

{data.table} is an R package that makes data wrangling operations extremely fast for large datasets. It will speed-up and RAM-down processing your big horrible datasets, your big horrible merge, your big horrible pivot, and your big horrible group-by aggregation.

If you can use data.table, then use {data.table}. If you find data.table syntax a bit baffling (or don’t want to invest the time to make it less baffling) and you’re familiar with dplyr and tidyr, then use {dtplyr}. {dtplyr} looks like dplyr but uses {data.table} under the hood. It’s a godsend for tidyverse aficionados.

Don’t ask for help with memory problems until you’ve first tried {data.table} or {dtplyr}! If you do, the answer will be “try data.table or dtplyr”.

You can see various examples of {dtplyr} in action in the covid-vax-history repository.

Get your ducks in a row

For genuinely large cohorts, how you store and read your data is often where the biggest wins hide — bigger than any amount of in-R micro-optimisation.

Reading text files (csv, tsv, …). The most common own-goal is letting read.csv() / read_csv() guess every column type from the data. Guessing is slow, and it routinely guesses wrong (an all-digits ID column becomes a double; a column that looks numeric until row 900,000 gets read as character). Tell it the types up front:

  • readr::read_csv(file, col_types = ...)

  • base read.csv(file, colClasses = ...)

  • or data.table::fread(), which is fast and types sensibly with little fuss.

This is faster, more reliable, and is itself a re-typing win (see Stay classy) — you read straight into integer/factor instead of reading wide and converting afterwards.

Columnar, compressed storage: parquet. If you control the file format, prefer parquet over csv for intermediate and large datasets. It’s columnar (so reading three columns out of fifty reads only those three — “column pushdown”), compressed (smaller on disk), typed (no guessing), and queryable lazily. The {arrow} package (in the v2 and v3 images) reads and writes it with arrow::write_parquet() / arrow::read_parquet(), or arrow::open_dataset() to query a whole directory of parquet files without loading them.

Larger-than-RAM querying: duckdb. This is arguably the single highest-leverage modern addition for an OpenSAFELY-scale workload. {duckdb} (also in the v2 and v3 images) is an in-process analytical database that plugs straight in as a {dbplyr} backend. You write ordinary dplyr, duckdb runs it — out-of-core, across multiple cores — and only the result you ask for is ever pulled into R, with collect(). You can query data frames already in memory…

library("dplyr")
library("duckdb")
Loading required package: DBI
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
duckdb_register(con, "dataset", dataset)   # registers the R object as a table, no copy

tbl(con, "dataset") |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_hba1c = mean(hba1c, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  sex        n mean_hba1c
  <fct>  <dbl>      <dbl>
1 female  4949       27.1
2 male    5051       27.2

…or, more powerfully, query parquet on disk that is never loaded into R at all — so the dataset can be far larger than your memory limit:

pq <- file.path(tempdir(), "cohort.parquet")

# write the cohort to parquet (here via duckdb; arrow::write_parquet() also works)
dbExecute(con, sprintf("COPY dataset TO '%s' (FORMAT parquet)", pq))
[1] 10000
# query the file lazily — only the filtered, aggregated result comes back into R
tbl(con, sprintf("read_parquet('%s')", pq)) |>
  filter(diabetes) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_hba1c = mean(hba1c, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
# A tibble: 1 × 2
      n mean_hba1c
  <dbl>      <dbl>
1  2076       34.9
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

Storing your big cohort as parquet and querying it with duckdb/dbplyr, pulling back only what you need, is the most powerful combination here for data that won’t fit in memory.

Saving R objects (models, lists, …): qs2. parquet is for tabular data; for everything else — fitted model objects, lists, imputation or bootstrap results — the usual saveRDS() is single-threaded and slow. {qs2} (in the v3 image) is a faster, smaller drop-in replacement: qs2::qs_save(obj, "file.qs2") and qs2::qs_read("file.qs2"). It’s handy for caching an expensive intermediate object so a later action can read it back quickly.

R image v3

OpenSAFELY R image version 3 will use OpenBLAS for linear algebra. This potentially results in operations that are orders of magnitude faster, and you don’t have to do anything! I don’t understand it, and neither you do, but that doesn’t mean we don’t get to benefit.

R v3 is not merged yet, but when it is, use it.

Don’t oversubscribe your cores

There is one catch worth knowing about. OpenBLAS is itself multithreaded — a single matrix operation can quietly use all your cores. That’s a free win when it’s the only thing running. But it can backfire when you combine it with explicit parallelisation: if you fit linear-algebra-heavy models (lots of glm()s, say) inside a {furrr} / {foreach} / {future.apply} cluster, you now have two layers fighting for the same cores. Each of your N worker processes spawns its own M OpenBLAS threads, and N × M can far exceed the number of cores you actually have. This oversubscription makes threads contend and context-switch, and can run slower than either layer on its own.

The fix is to control the nesting — usually, turn BLAS threading down to 1 while you parallelise explicitly, so each worker stays single-threaded:

# In the v3 image, from within R:
library("RhpcBLASctl")
blas_set_num_threads(1)   # stop each worker spawning its own BLAS threads
# ... now launch your furrr / foreach / future.apply cluster ...

On any image you can do the same thing from the shell before R starts, by setting an environment variable — OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 or OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1.

The flip side: if your bottleneck is a single big matrix operation and you are not parallelising explicitly, do the opposite — leave OpenBLAS free to use all the cores and don’t set up a cluster at all.

A sample is ample

You probably don’t need to include all of the patients that you could be using. Certainly not during the first development cycle. In some cases, even after trying everything else above, you still won’t be able to run your code on the full cohort of patients. So consider sampling.

There are different approaches to this, from pure random sampling (take 10% of your cohort, for speed 90% gains), to more sophisticated approaches depending on the analytic task, where your statistical power is coming from, and which bits are slow.

For example, if we’re studying a cohort of 10m patients, but the outcome is extremely rare, occurring in just 100 patients. Then randomly sampling 10% of the cohort would leave us with about 10 outcome events, seriously harming statistical power. Instead, we could keep all 100 patients who experienced the outcome, but sample 10% from the remaining 9999900 event-free patients, leaving 999990. The analysis will need to be weighted to recover the right estimates. We weight by the inverse of the sampling probability, so in the example above, patients with the event have weight \(w_{y=1} = 1 / 1 = 1\), and event-free patients have weight \(w_{y=0} = 1/0.1 = 10\).

Ruth Keogh has a paper coming out about this in the next few weeks.

Things to avoid

  • rowwise() — it processes a data frame one row at a time, the very opposite of vectorisation. Reach for vectorised functions, dplyr::across(), or, if you genuinely need a row-wise operation, purrr::pmap().

  • apply() on a data frame — it silently coerces the whole thing to a matrix first, so a single character column drags every column to character. Use column-wise tools instead (dplyr::across(), purrr::map(), lapply()).

  • do.call(rbind, ...), or rbind() / bind_rows() inside a loop — this is the same quadratic-copying trap as Copy that. Collect the pieces into a list and combine them once at the end with dplyr::bind_rows(), purrr::list_rbind(), or data.table::rbindlist().

  • ifelse() on large vectors — it’s slower than it needs to be and type-unstable (it can strip attributes and coerce types). Prefer dplyr::if_else() (strict about types), or dplyr::case_when() when there are several conditions.

  • <<- (super-assignment) — it reaches up into an enclosing or global scope to modify a variable, which is hard to reason about and easy to get wrong. It’s often a sign of an accumulation pattern that would be better as a vectorised operation or a pre-allocated result.

More stuff

A note on costs. Data platforms that cost based on data storage and compute are not uncommon. The flat-rate £25k/year OS costing model is not necessarily permanent, and it may move to a compute-based costing model in future (pure speculation! but don’t rule it out).
